questions.difficultyReason: Students must identify the zero-normal-force threshold and link it to the largest downward SHM acceleration.

explanation.body: At the top of the motion, the downward force equation is $ma=mg-N$. At the limiting amplitude $N=0$, so $m\omega^2x_0=mg$. Hence $x_0=g/\omega^2=g/(2\pi f)^2=9.81/[4\pi^2(2.0)^2]=6.2\ \mathrm{cm}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.B: Sets the limit at a downward acceleration below free fall, so the object still presses on the platform.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The presence of repeated cycles with decreasing amplitude identifies the damping regime.
questions.misconception: Inferring the damping regime from the liquid’s viscosity alone.

explanation.body: The block completes several oscillations while viscous forces dissipate its mechanical energy. Its amplitude decreases until it is effectively at rest, which is characteristic of light damping.

perOption.A: Critical damping returns the block to equilibrium without repeated oscillations.
perOption.B: Heavy damping gives a slower, nonoscillatory return to equilibrium.
perOption.C: Correct. Oscillations persist while their amplitude decreases.
perOption.D: Without damping, the oscillations would continue at constant amplitude.

questions.difficultyReason: Squaring the SHM speed relation gives the energy ratio directly.
questions.misconception: Using the speed ratio as the energy ratio

The speed v of the water waves is given by = v gd where g is the acceleration due to gravity and d is the depth of the water in the tank. If the depth of the water in the tank is 0.30 m, what is the wavelength of the water waves when the cork is moving up and down with the largest amplitude? A 0.070 m B 0.14 m C 0.21 m D 0.35 m

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must link resonance to the natural frequency and then combine with a given wave-speed formula.
questions.misconception: Not recognising that maximum amplitude means driving frequency equals natural frequency

explanation.body:
The cork vibrates with maximum amplitude at resonance, when the wave period equals the cork's natural period, $T = 0.12$ s.

perOption.B: Does not follow from $\lambda = vT$ with $v = \sqrt{gd}$.
perOption.C: Correct. Resonance: wave period equals the natural period.
perOption.D: Forgets the square root: $Tgd \approx 0.35$ m.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert scale readings into displacements from equilibrium and solve two inverse-cosine equations.
questions.misconception: Measuring displacement from the end of the scale rather than from equilibrium

explanation.body:
Amplitude $x_0 = \dfrac{2.00}{2} = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}$, with the equilibrium position at the 1.00 m mark. So the 0.75 m mark is at $x = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ and the 1.50 m mark is at $x = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$.

Taking the swing to be at the 0 m mark at $t = 0$: $x = -1.00\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{2.4}t\right)$

At $x = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}$: $t_1 = 0.5035\ \mathrm{s}$. At $x = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$: $t_2 = 0.8000\ \mathrm{s}$.

questions.stemText:
A body oscillates in simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation with displacement $x$ of the velocity $v$ of the body.

[Graph: $v$ / m s$^{-1}$ against $x$ / m is an ellipse centred at the origin, crossing the $x$-axis at $-0.50$ and $0.50$ and the $v$-axis at $2.0$ and $-2.0$.]

The body is now made to oscillate such that its amplitude is reduced to 0.25 m, while maintaining the same total mechanical energy.

What is the new maximum acceleration of the body?

A $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$   B $8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$   C $16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$   D $32\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: A body oscillates in simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation with displacement x of the velocity v of the body. v / m s−1 2.0 x / m 0 −0.50 0.50 −

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must read $x_0$ and $v_0$ from the ellipse and realise that constant energy forces $\omega$ to change.
questions.misconception: Assuming the angular frequency stays the same when the amplitude changes

explanation.body:
From the graph, $x_0 = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ and $v_0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $\omega = \dfrac{v_0}{x_0} = \dfrac{2.0}{0.50} = 4.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

Total energy $E_T = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$. Since $E_T$ and $m$ are constant, $\omega x_0$ stays constant:

$\omega' x_0' = \omega x_0 \Rightarrow \omega' = \dfrac{4.0 \times 0.50}{0.25} = 8.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

$|a_0| = (\omega')^2 x_0' = 8.0^2 \times 0.25 = 16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

perOption.A: Keeps $\omega = 4.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ unchanged and uses the new amplitude: $4.0^2 \times 0.25$.
perOption.B: Gives the original maximum acceleration, $4.0^2 \times 0.50$.
perOption.C: Correct. Constant energy keeps $\omega x_0$ fixed, so $\omega$ doubles.
perOption.D: Uses the new $\omega' = 8.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ with the old amplitude of 0.50 m.

A N mg x $-x_{o}$ 0 $x_{o}$ B N mg x $-x_{o}$ 0 $x_{o}$ C  D

questions.difficultyReason: Must apply $a=-\omega^2 x$ with Newton's second law at the extremes and map it to a graph.
questions.misconception: Thinks contact force is largest at the top or always equals $mg$.

explanation.body:
At equilibrium ($x=0$), $a=0$ so $N = mg$.

At $x=+x_0$ (top), $mg - N = ma$, so $N = mg - mg = 0$.

At $x=-x_0$ (bottom), $N - mg = ma$, so $N = mg + mg = 2mg$.

So $N$ falls linearly from $2mg$ at $-x_0$ through $mg$ at $0$ to $0$ at $+x_0$, which is graph C.

perOption.A: Shows $N$ peaking at $mg$ at $x=0$ and falling at both ends, but $N$ is linear in $x$ and equals $0$ only at the top.
perOption.B: Has $N=0$ at $x=0$, but the sand is in equilibrium there so $N=mg$.
perOption.C: Correct. Straight line decreasing from $2mg$ to $0$.
perOption.D: Slopes the wrong way: gives $N=0$ at the bottom and $2mg$ at the top.

explanation.body:

explanation.body:
$ma = mg - R$. The object loses contact when $R = 0$, so $ma = mg$.

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must distinguish changes in peak height, width and frequency.
questions.misconception: Reducing damping shifts resonance to a lower frequency.

explanation.body: Reducing damping reduces energy loss, increasing the amplitude near resonance. The resonance peak narrows and shifts towards the undamped natural frequency, which is higher than the damped peak frequency. Only statement 3 is correct.

perOption.A: Statement 1 reverses the effect of lower damping on the amplitude near resonance.
perOption.B: Statement 2 reverses the shift of the peak frequency.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Includes statements 1 and 2, which reverse the changes in amplitude and peak frequency.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows the variation with displacement x of the velocity v of a body undergoing simple harmonic motion.

What is the time for the body to take to reduce its speed from maximum to zero?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows the variation with displacement x of the velocity v of a body undergoing simple harmonic motion. v / m s−1 20 x / m −4.0 4.0 −20 What is the time for the body to take to reduce its speed from maximum to zero? A 0.20 s B 0.31 s C 1.3 s D 4.0 s

appearances.originalFile: grail:15121 TMJC_2024_H2 Physics P1_QP_AS

questions.difficultyReason: Requires extracting $x_0$ and $v_0$ from a $v$–$x$ graph and knowing max-to-zero speed is a quarter cycle.
questions.misconception: taking the full period instead of a quarter period

explanation.body:
From the graph, amplitude $x_0 = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and maximum speed $v_0 = 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$v_0 = \omega x_0 \Rightarrow 20 = \omega \times 4.0$, so $\omega = 5.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{5.0} = 1.257\ \mathrm{s}$.

Speed goes from maximum (at equilibrium) to zero (at the extreme) in $\tfrac{1}{4}T = 0.31\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Gives $1/\omega$ instead of a quarter period.
perOption.B: Correct. $\tfrac{1}{4}T = \tfrac{1}{4}(2\pi/5.0) = 0.31\ \mathrm{s}$.
perOption.C: This is the full period; maximum to zero speed takes only a quarter period.
perOption.D: Reads the amplitude in metres as a time.

explanation.body: For amplitude $x_0$, the total energy is $E_{\mathrm T}=\frac12m\omega^2x_0^2$. At $x=x_0/2$, $E_{\mathrm K}=\frac12m\omega^2[x_0^2-(x_0/2)^2]=\frac34E_{\mathrm T}$. Since $E_{\mathrm T}=E_{\mathrm K}+E_{\mathrm P}$, $E_{\mathrm P}=\frac14E_{\mathrm T}$.

questions.stemText:
A particle oscillates with simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation, with time $t$, of the potential energy of the particle from $t = 0$ to $t = 2$ s.

[Graph: potential energy against $t$/s; PE starts at a maximum at $t = 0$, falls smoothly to zero at $t = 1$ s, and rises back to the maximum at $t = 2$ s.]

Which graph could represent the variation, with time $t$, of the velocity $v$ of the particle from $t = 0$ to $t = 2$ s?

A [$v$–$t$: starts at 0, one full sine cycle (positive peak then negative trough) ending at 0 at $t = 2$ s]
B [$v$–$t$: starts at a positive maximum, one full cosine cycle down to a negative minimum and back to the maximum at $t = 2$ s]
C [$v$–$t$: starts at 0, rises to a single positive maximum at $t = 1$ s, returns to 0 at $t = 2$ s]
D [$v$–$t$: starts at a positive maximum, falls through zero at $t = 1$ s to a negative minimum at $t = 2$ s]

stemImage.alt: Question 16: A particle oscillates with simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation, with time t, of the potential energy of the particle from t = 0 to t = 2 s. Wh

appearances.originalFile: grail:19928 VJC 2025 J2 H2 Phy Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires realising PE has twice the frequency of the motion, so the 2 s window is only half a period.
questions.misconception: Assuming the energy graph has the same period as the oscillation

explanation.body:
The given PE graph shows only half a period of the oscillation: PE goes from maximum (at an extreme) to zero (at equilibrium) and back to maximum (at the other extreme).

$PE \propto \cos^2\omega t$, so $KE \propto \sin^2\omega t$, giving $v \propto \sin\omega t$, i.e. $v = v_0\sin\omega t$.

Over half a period, $v$ rises from zero to a maximum and returns to zero without changing sign. Option C shows exactly this half-period $v$–$t$ graph.

perOption.A: Shows a full period of $v$ over 2 s; PE would then complete two cycles in 2 s.
perOption.B: Starts at maximum velocity, but PE is maximum (so $v = 0$) at $t = 0$; it also shows a full period.
perOption.C: Correct. Half a period of $v = v_0\sin\omega t$.
perOption.D: Starts at maximum velocity, but at $t = 0$ PE is maximum so $v$ must be zero.

questions.stemText: A particle of mass 4.0 kg moves with simple harmonic motion and its potential energy U varies with position x as shown in the figure below. What is the period of oscillation of the particle? A 0.25 s B 0.89 s C 1.8 s D 2.5 s

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must read an energy–position pair and connect it to angular frequency and period.
questions.misconception: Using the full horizontal span as the displacement.

explanation.body: From the graph, $U=1.0\ \mathrm{J}$ at $x=0.2\ \mathrm{m}$. Using the SHM energy relation and $\omega=2\pi/T$ gives $1.0=\tfrac12(4.0)(2\pi/T)^2(0.2)^2$. Solving gives $T=1.78\ \mathrm{s}$, or $1.8\ \mathrm{s}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Gives a period that predicts a potential energy far above 1.0 J at the marked displacement.
perOption.B: Halves the calculated full period.
perOption.C: Correct. The energy–position pair gives a period of about 1.8 s.
perOption.D: Is consistent with omitting the factor of one half in the energy formula.

What is the maximum kinetic energy of the particle?

A $2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J}$  B $2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J}$  C $3.9\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J}$  D $5.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J}$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: A particle of mass 5.0  10–3 kg performing simple harmonic motion takes 47 s to make 50 oscillations. In each complete oscillation, the particle travels a tota

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Requires deducing amplitude from distance per cycle and chaining frequency, angular frequency and KE.
questions.misconception: Taking the distance per oscillation as two amplitudes rather than four

explanation.body:
Amplitude: $x_0 = 600/4 = 150\ \mathrm{mm} = 0.150\ \mathrm{m}$ (one oscillation covers four amplitudes).

Frequency: $f = 50/47 = 1.064\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so $\omega = 2\pi f = 6.684\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

Max KE $= \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2x_0^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(5.0\times10^{-3})(6.684)^2(0.150)^2 = 2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J}$

perOption.A: Uses $f = 47/50$ (inverting the frequency).
perOption.B: Correct. $x_0 = 0.150\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\omega = 6.684\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Results from an incorrect amplitude or angular frequency.
perOption.D: Omits the factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the kinetic energy.

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the effect of damping on a resonance curve.

explanation.body: With greater damping, more energy is lost per cycle, so the amplitude of the forced oscillations is lower at all frequencies (the resonance peak is lower and flatter).

perOption.A: Correct. More damping reduces amplitude across the response curve.
perOption.B: Damping removes energy, so it cannot raise the amplitude.
perOption.C: Damping lowers the curve below resonance as well, especially at the peak.
perOption.D: Damping never increases amplitude.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires inferring relative damping from free oscillations and applying it to forced response curves.
questions.misconception: Expecting stronger damping to raise the resonance peak.

explanation.body: Q's free oscillations die away faster, so Q is more strongly damped. Its frequency-response curve lies below P's at positive driving frequencies, which rules out A and B. Q has a lower peak at a slightly lower frequency than P.

perOption.A: Shows Q above P over parts of the frequency range.
perOption.B: Shows Q crossing above P and peaking at a higher frequency.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the more strongly damped Q a taller peak.
